# About this course {.unnumbered}

In chemistry, too, "AI" seems to be everywhere. It is in the news, in all the journals, in all the proposals. It is also at the heart of the research my group does. But I think that there is a lot of nuance to it. An my hope is that this course will give you a chance to explore that nuance, and to practise the skills that let you make your own judgements about what a model does and what its results establish.

My starting point is that AI is a deeply human endeavour. Someone decides which question is worth asking. Someone produces the measurements, chooses what the model should learn, and decides what counts as a good answer. Much of this work may have happened before we download a dataset or open a chatbot. It has still happened. Automating part of the calculation does not remove the decisions that made it possible.

Consider a molecular drawing. It records atoms and bonds but usually leaves out the solvent and temperature (and even the concept of a structure itself is a [conventient fiction](https://pubs.acs.org/jacsat/article/100/4/1073/552820/Must-a-molecule-have-a-shape)). For discussing connectivity, that may be enough. Now ask how much of the molecule dissolves. The drawing has not changed, but what we need to know has. Modelling means leaving things out; the difficult part is deciding which omissions we can afford for the question we want to answer.

This is also why I find AI more useful as the name of an ambition than as the subject of a precise conversation. Building systems with capabilities we associate with intelligence leaves room for very different methods. Many of the ambitions are old; some of the ways we can now pursue them are new. The [opening lecture](lectures/01-ai-and-science.qmd) asks what these systems actually do, and how that compares with the scientific claims and commercial promises made about them.


## What should you be able to do afterwards? {#course-outcomes}

By the end of the course, I would like you to be able to:

- Turn a chemical question into a modelling task, and explain what information you have kept and what you have left out.
- Build and compare small models in Python, choosing an evaluation that makes sense for the intended use. Explain why even a carefully reserved test set gives an empirical estimate.
- Distinguish predicting an outcome, explaining a model's calculation, and establishing what an intervention would cause. Say what evidence your own conclusion needs.
- Use an LLM or coding assistant to help with the work, while being able to check the calculations and defend the choices yourself.

These are also the things I would like your project to let you practise. 

## The course sequence

[]{#our-first-hands-on-example}

We first learn to fit a small model and examine the evidence for using it. We then study how models represent molecules and their behaviour. Finally, we ask how predictions can help us propose molecules, choose experiments, and organise a research task. A small project brings the calculation and its scientific interpretation together.

| Topic groups | Main topics |
|---|---|
| **1–3: Learning from observations** | AI and scientific claims; our computing tools; fitting and evaluating models; chemical data. |
| **4–6: Representing molecules and their behaviour** | Neural networks; molecular graphs and symmetry; learned energies, forces, and simulation. |
| **7–9: From predictions to decisions** | Molecular generation; choosing experiments under uncertainty; language models and tools. |
| **10: Bringing the work together** | Reproducing, explaining, and examining a small project. |

Friedolin lists **14 two-hour meetings** from 28 October to 10 February. I cannot teach on 4 November, which leaves **13 meetings, including the introduction**. The [course outline](outline.qmd) distributes the ten topic groups and three further practical and project meetings across that time. In the first session, we will [discuss a block week or several longer sessions](outline.qmd#scheduling), working around my unavailable dates and students' commitments.

## How we will work {#how-to-use-a-lecture-page}

These notes are for master's students in chemistry. We develop the Python and machine-learning ideas alongside the chemical problems, starting with small examples. In the first meeting, on **Wednesday, 28 October 2026, 14:00–16:00, at Helmholtzweg 4, SR 6 Physik**, I would like to hear what you most want to learn and discuss a course format that works for us. We will begin with AI, prediction, and the human choices behind models, then see our tools in use and spend about half an hour setting them up together. You can [try the setup beforehand](setup.qmd), but a working installation is not required to join the first session. The [course outline](outline.qmd#scheduling) collects the dates and formats we will discuss.

For the meetings after this introduction, I would like to propose a short introduction from me, perhaps ten to fifteen minutes, followed by plenty of time for you to work through examples and your own calculations. I will work with you as questions arise, help debug code, and discuss what the results mean. If several people run into the same difficulty, we can pause for a short explanation together. We will discuss whether this format would work for you in the first meeting.

Later, more of that work will happen in Python notebooks. A short preparation task can help us get started; an unfinished attempt gives us something to work on together. We will also use large language models for help with code and explanations. That gives us another model to question: did its suggestion help, and how do we know?

The [assessment](outline.qmd#assessment) consists of a project with a written report and a final presentation with discussion. I would like the writing and presentation to grow out of work you find interesting. We will discuss a manageable scope, format, and timing together in the first meeting.

The [glossary](glossary.qmd) explains technical terms with examples from chemistry and our computing tools. Linked terms in the notes take you directly to the relevant entry.

Several books have shaped how I think about these questions. I particularly recommend Hardt and Recht's *Patterns, Predictions, and Actions*, Kate Crawford's *Atlas of AI*, Carissa Véliz's *Prophecy*, and Simon J. D. Prince's *Understanding Deep Learning*. For an introduction to machine learning, I also recommend [our review on porous materials and Mehta and colleagues' introduction for physicists](reading.qmd#introductory-reviews). These and the papers discussed in class are collected under [suggested reading](reading.qmd). The reading is optional.

## The course material {#start-here}

- [Course outline](outline.qmd): the topics, proposed timetable, and background developed along the way.
- [AI-assistant and Python setup](setup.qmd): Jan with Blablador as one option for an assistant, then computing basics, uv, and marimo, with a downloadable introductory kit. Windows users work in Ubuntu on WSL 2.
- [What do we mean by AI for science?](lectures/01-ai-and-science.qmd): AI as an ambition, concrete methods, a selective history, and scientific evidence.
- [What does it mean to learn from data?](lectures/02-learning-from-data.qmd): a calibration experiment, choosing how to measure an error, fitting curves, and predicting new measurements.
- [What can a model tell us about gas uptake?](lectures/03-mof-uptake.qmd): describing porous materials to a computer, comparing predictions, and examining the uncertainty in an error estimate.
- [Examples from chemistry](examples.qmd): chemical applications used to examine what a method does and what its results establish.
- [Glossary](glossary.qmd): descriptors, features, parameters, kernels, and other terms used in the notes.
- [Suggested reading](reading.qmd): books I recommend and the sources behind the examples.

## Examples from chemistry {#examples-through-lenses}

The [collection of chemical applications](examples.qmd) lets us ask what was done and what the result establishes, using the distinctions introduced in lecture 1.

[]{#choices-within-a-lens}

The [solubility example](examples.qmd#choices-within-a-lens) makes a smaller decision consequential. We have measured a value. Should we keep it, replace it with “soluble enough,” or keep only the order of the molecules? The answer changes which questions we can ask of the resulting data.

## Your feedback {#feedback}

This is the first time I am teaching this course here in Jena. It is also a time when many of the methods and tools we will discuss are changing quickly. I have been trying out LLMs in other courses, but I am still working out where they help students learn and where they get in the way. This course will be part of that process.

I would therefore really appreciate your feedback throughout the course. Tell me what works and what does not. Perhaps an explanation assumes something we have not covered, or an assistant helps you finish a calculation without helping you understand it. Knowing where that happens gives me a chance to adjust the teaching while it can still help you.

I will leave a little time at the end of our meetings for two questions: **What helped you understand something? What got in the way?** You can also tell me during class, afterwards, or in a short message. Feedback is optional and is not part of the assessment -- but I value your input *a lot*.

## How these notes were written {#about-these-notes}

These lecture notes were developed through an ongoing, iterative dialogue with OpenAI's Codex. I used it to help structure the course, draft and revise explanations, and develop code and teaching activities, drawing on my earlier teaching material and the sources cited throughout the notes. I guide the course's content and teaching approach and remain responsible for the material, including any errors.

This is also part of what we will discuss in the course: how to use an assistant while retaining judgement about the question, the reasoning, and the evidence. Please point out errors or unclear explanations so that we can improve the notes.
